concept.name: Sandwich attack
concept.definition: A sandwich attack is an MEV strategy in which an attacker sees a victim's pending DEX trade in the mempool, inserts a buy immediately before it (front-run) and a sell immediately after it (back-run), profiting from the price movement the victim's own trade creates.
concept.intuition: A predator spots your big market order in the waiting room, jumps the queue to buy ahead of you, lets your purchase push the price up, then dumps on you — you become their exit liquidity.
concept.mechanics: The searcher computes the victim trade's price impact, front-runs with a buy that raises the price, lets the victim's trade execute at a worse rate (bounded only by their slippage tolerance), then back-runs with a sell at the elevated price. The profit comes directly from the victim's worse execution, net of gas and bribes to builders for ordering.
concept.failure_modes: Sandwiches are not atomic, so the attacker bears inventory risk if the back-run fails or another bot interferes (e.g. 'salmonella' counter-attacks); tight victim slippage settings can make the attack unprofitable.
concept.misconceptions: Sandwiching is not hacking the victim's wallet — it exploits the public ordering of otherwise valid transactions. High slippage tolerance is the attacker's margin; private transaction relays mitigate but centralize order flow.
concept.example: A user buys 10,000 UNI with DAI on Uniswap with 5% slippage; a bot front-runs a UNI buy, the user's trade executes near the worst allowed price, and the bot's immediate sell extracts the difference — the user receives materially fewer UNI than quoted.

citations.source: Ethereum.org developer docs - Maximal extractable value (MEV)
